question: To prevent sympathetic ophthalmia after a severe penetrating ocular injury to one eye, the injured (exciting) eye should be eviscerated rather than enucleated, because evisceration preserves the scleral shell and thus provides better orbital volume for a prosthesis.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Correct — FALSE. Evisceration retains the sclera AND the uveal remnants, which can still trigger sympathetic ophthalmia. Enucleation removes the entire globe including all uveal tissue and is the gold standard for sympathetic ophthalmia prevention after a penetrating exciting-eye injury. Prosthetic fit is addressed separately.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Incorrect — the statement is FALSE. Evisceration leaves uveal tissue behind inside the scleral shell, and this retained uveal tissue is the very antigen that triggers sympathetic ophthalmia. Enucleation (complete globe removal) is the procedure that eliminates the risk. Evisceration is CONTRAINDICATED when sympathetic ophthalmia is a concern.
